blocks.body:
Here is a typical extremal question. A town has $n$ residents who form clubs. Every club has an odd number of members, and any two clubs share an even number of members. How many clubs can there be? Counting arguments struggle with conditions like this. Linear algebra settles it in a few lines: at most $n$.

The method always has the same shape. Attach to each member of the family a vector, or a polynomial, in a vector space whose dimension you know. Use the combinatorial hypothesis to prove that these vectors are linearly independent. Then the family is no larger than the dimension. This lesson develops the method through three results: the Oddtown theorem, Fisher's inequality and the Frankl–Wilson theorem.

blocks.title: The dimension argument
blocks.body:
The one fact from linear algebra we need is the key statement of [[basis-dimension]]: in a vector space of dimension $n$ over a field $\mathbb F$, a linearly independent list has at most $n$ vectors,
$$v_1,\dots,v_m \in \mathbb F^n \text{ independent} \Rightarrow m \le n.$$

To use it on a family of subsets $A_1, \dots, A_m$ of $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$, represent each set by its characteristic vector $v_i \in \mathbb F^n$, whose $k$-th coordinate is $1$ if $k \in A_i$ and $0$ otherwise. The point of this choice is that the dot product counts intersections:
$$v_i \cdot v_j = |A_i \cap A_j|,$$
computed in the integers or the reals, or reduced modulo $2$ if $\mathbb F = \mathbb F_2$ is the field with two elements ([[finite-fields]]).

The standard way to prove independence is through the Gram matrix $G = (v_i \cdot v_j)_{i,j}$. Suppose $\sum_i c_i v_i = 0$. Taking the dot product with $v_j$ gives $\sum_i c_i\,(v_i\cdot v_j) = 0$ for each $j$, that is, $Gc = 0$. So if $G$ is invertible ([[determinants]]), then $c = 0$ and the vectors are independent. Only bilinearity of the dot product is used, so this works over any field, including $\mathbb F_2$, where the dot product is not an inner product in the geometric sense: a non-zero vector can have $v \cdot v = 0$.

blocks.title: Oddtown theorem
blocks.body: Let $A_1, \dots, A_m \subseteq [n]$ be such that $|A_i|$ is odd for every $i$ and $|A_i \cap A_j|$ is even for all $i \ne j$. Then $m \le n$.

Work over $\mathbb F_2$. The Gram matrix of the characteristic vectors has diagonal entries $|A_i| \equiv 1$ and off-diagonal entries $|A_i \cap A_j| \equiv 0 \pmod 2$, so it is the identity matrix. It is invertible, so $v_1, \dots, v_m$ are independent in $\mathbb F_2^n$, and $m \le n$. (The sets are automatically distinct, since $A_i = A_j$ would give an odd intersection.) The $n$ singletons show that the bound is attained.

blocks.title: Why the field and the hypothesis matter
blocks.body:
Swap the parity of the sizes. In Eventown every club has an even number of members and every two clubs share an even number. Now the Gram matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ is zero and the argument collapses, rightly so. Pair up the residents as $\{1,2\}, \{3,4\}, \dots$ and let the clubs be all unions of pairs. Sizes and intersections are even, and there are $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ clubs, exponentially many.

Linear algebra still gives the right answer for Eventown, by a different argument. All characteristic vectors satisfy $v_i\cdot v_j = 0$, including $i = j$, so their span $W$ satisfies $W \subseteq W^\perp$, where $W^\perp = \{x : x\cdot w = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}$. If $W$ has dimension $d$, then $W^\perp$ is the solution space of $d$ independent linear equations (one for each vector of a basis of $W$), so it has dimension $n - d$. From $W \subseteq W^\perp$ we get $d \le n - d$, so $d \le n/2$. The family lies inside $W$, which has $2^d$ elements, so $m \le 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, matching the construction.

So the field must fit the hypothesis: parity conditions call for $\mathbb F_2$, while exact equalities usually call for $\mathbb R$, where positive definiteness is available.

blocks.title: Fisher's inequality
blocks.body: Let $\lambda \ge 1$ and let $A_1, \dots, A_m$ be distinct subsets of $[n]$ with $|A_i \cap A_j| = \lambda$ for all $i \ne j$. Then $m \le n$.

Work over $\mathbb R$. Suppose first that $|A_i| > \lambda$ for every $i$, and put $d_i = |A_i| - \lambda > 0$. The Gram matrix is $G = D + \lambda J$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $d_i$ and $J$ is the all-ones matrix. For any real vector $x \ne 0$,
$$x^{T} G x = \sum_i d_i x_i^2 + \lambda\Big(\sum_i x_i\Big)^2 > 0,$$
so $Gx \ne 0$. Hence $G$ is invertible, the $v_i$ are independent in $\mathbb R^n$, and $m \le n$.

Now suppose some set, say $A_1$, has exactly $\lambda$ elements. Then $|A_1 \cap A_j| = \lambda = |A_1|$ forces $A_1 \subseteq A_j$ for all $j$. For distinct $i, j \ge 2$ the intersection $A_i \cap A_j$ contains $A_1$ and has $\lambda$ elements, so it equals $A_1$. Thus the sets $A_j \setminus A_1$ for $j \ge 2$ are pairwise disjoint, and they are non-empty because $A_j \ne A_1$. They live in the $n - \lambda$ elements outside $A_1$, so $m - 1 \le n - \lambda \le n - 1$.

blocks.title: Small towns
blocks.body: For $n = 4$, find the largest Oddtown family and the largest Eventown family, and compare with the bounds above.
blocks.solution:
Oddtown: the bound is $4$, and the four singletons attain it. Another extremal family is $\{1,2,3\}, \{1,2,4\}, \{1,3,4\}, \{2,3,4\}$: each set has $3$ elements and any two share $2$.

Eventown: the bound is $2^{\lfloor 4/2\rfloor} = 4$, attained by $\emptyset, \{1,2\}, \{3,4\}, \{1,2,3,4\}$. This family is closed under symmetric difference, so it is exactly a $2$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb F_2^4$, as the proof predicts for a family of the maximal size $2^d$.

blocks.title: The Fano plane
blocks.body: The Fano plane has points $1, \dots, 7$ and seven lines $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{1,4,5\}$, $\{1,6,7\}$, $\{2,4,6\}$, $\{2,5,7\}$, $\{3,4,7\}$, $\{3,5,6\}$. Check that it attains equality in Fisher's inequality, and compute the determinant of its Gram matrix.
blocks.solution:
Each line has $3$ points and any two lines meet in exactly one point; for instance $\{1,4,5\} \cap \{2,5,7\} = \{5\}$, and all $21$ pairs can be checked the same way. So $\lambda = 1$ and $m = 7 = n$: Fisher's inequality is sharp.

The Gram matrix is $G = 2I + J$, with diagonal entries $3$ and all other entries $1$. The all-ones vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $2 + 7 = 9$, and every vector with coordinate sum $0$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $2$; these form a $6$-dimensional space. Hence
$$\det G = 2^6 \cdot 9 = 576 \ne 0,$$
confirming that the seven characteristic vectors are independent in $\mathbb R^7$.

Fisher proved his inequality in 1940 for block designs (a design has at least as many blocks as points); the version above, with no condition on set sizes, is the non-uniform Fisher inequality.

blocks.title: Equal unions
blocks.body:
Let $A_1, \dots, A_{n+1}$ be non-empty subsets of $[n]$. Prove that there are disjoint non-empty sets of indices $I, J \subseteq \{1, \dots, n+1\}$ with
$$\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{j \in J} A_j.$$
blocks.solution:
The $n+1$ characteristic vectors $v_1, \dots, v_{n+1}$ lie in $\mathbb R^n$, so they are linearly dependent: $\sum_i c_i v_i = 0$ with real $c_i$ not all zero. Let $I = \{i : c_i > 0\}$ and $J = \{j : c_j < 0\}$; these are disjoint. Moving the negative terms to the other side,
$$\sum_{i\in I} c_i v_i = \sum_{j \in J} (-c_j)\, v_j.$$
All coefficients on both sides are positive and all vectors have non-negative entries. If $I$ were empty, the left side would be $0$; but a positive combination of non-zero $0/1$ vectors is non-zero unless it is empty, so $J$ would be empty too, contradicting that some $c_i \ne 0$. By the same argument $J$ is non-empty.

Now compare supports. Coordinate $k$ of the left side is positive exactly when $k \in A_i$ for some $i \in I$, because the coefficients are positive and the entries non-negative; similarly for the right side and $J$. Equal vectors have equal supports, so $\bigcup_{i\in I} A_i = \bigcup_{j\in J} A_j$.

blocks.title: Polynomials as vectors
blocks.body:
Vectors need not be lists of numbers. Functions form vector spaces too, and evaluating them at points is a flexible way to prove independence. Suppose functions $f_1, \dots, f_m$ and points $u_1, \dots, u_m$ satisfy $f_i(u_i) \ne 0$ for all $i$ and $f_i(u_j) = 0$ whenever $j < i$. Then the $f_i$ are linearly independent. Indeed, if $\sum_i c_i f_i = 0$, evaluating at $u_1$ kills every term except $c_1 f_1(u_1)$, so $c_1 = 0$; then evaluating at $u_2$ gives $c_2 = 0$, and so on.

For subsets of $[n]$ the relevant points are the vertices of the cube $\{0,1\}^n$, the characteristic vectors. On these points $x_k^2 = x_k$, so any polynomial can be replaced by a multilinear one, in which no variable appears with exponent above $1$, taking the same values on the cube and of no larger degree. The multilinear polynomials of degree at most $s$ in $n$ variables are spanned by the monomials $\prod_{k \in S} x_k$ with $|S| \le s$, so they form a space of dimension $\sum_{i=0}^{s}\binom ni$.

blocks.title: Frankl–Wilson theorem
blocks.body:
Let $L$ be a set of $s$ non-negative integers, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of subsets of $[n]$ such that $|A \cap B| \in L$ for all distinct $A, B \in \mathcal F$. Then
$$|\mathcal F| \le \sum_{i=0}^{s}\binom ni.$$

List the members of $\mathcal F$ as $A_1, \dots, A_m$ with $|A_1| \le |A_2| \le \dots \le |A_m|$, and let $v_1, \dots, v_m \in \{0,1\}^n$ be their characteristic vectors. For each $i$ define a polynomial in $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ by
$$f_i(x) = \prod_{\ell \in L,\ \ell < |A_i|} (v_i\cdot x - \ell).$$
It is a product of at most $s$ linear factors, so it has degree at most $s$.

At its own point, $f_i(v_i) = \prod (|A_i| - \ell)$ is a product of positive numbers, so $f_i(v_i) \ne 0$. For $j < i$ we have $|A_j| \le |A_i|$ and $A_j \ne A_i$, so $A_i \not\subseteq A_j$ and therefore $\ell_0 = |A_i \cap A_j| < |A_i|$. Since $\ell_0 \in L$, the factor $v_i\cdot x - \ell_0$ occurs in $f_i$, and it vanishes at $x = v_j$. So $f_i(v_j) = 0$ for all $j < i$.

By the triangular criterion above, $f_1, \dots, f_m$ are linearly independent as functions on $\{0,1\}^n$. Replace each $f_i$ by its multilinear reduction $\tilde f_i$. These agree with the $f_i$ on the cube, so they are still independent, and they lie in the space of multilinear polynomials of degree at most $s$, which has dimension $\sum_{i=0}^{s}\binom ni$. Hence $m \le \sum_{i=0}^s \binom ni$.

The bound is sharp. For $L = \{0, 1, \dots, s-1\}$, the family of all subsets of $[n]$ with at most $s$ elements has exactly $\sum_{i=0}^s\binom ni$ members, and two distinct such sets meet in at most $s - 1$ elements. When all members of $\mathcal F$ have the same size, the bound improves to $\binom ns$; this uniform version is due to Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson (1975). Frankl and Wilson (1981) also proved a modular version, in which the sizes and intersections are only controlled modulo a prime.

- Over $\mathbb F_2$ a non-zero vector can be orthogonal to itself, so "pairwise orthogonal non-zero vectors are independent" is false there, as Eventown shows. The argument needs non-zero diagonal entries.
- Forgetting the multilinear reduction. All polynomials of degree at most $s$ in $n$ variables form a space of dimension $\binom{n+s}{s}$, which gives a weaker bound.
- Dropping the ordering by size in the Frankl–Wilson proof. Without it, $f_i(v_j)$ need not vanish when $A_i \subset A_j$.
- Applying Fisher's inequality with $\lambda = 0$. Pairwise disjoint sets can number $n + 1$: the $n$ singletons and the empty set.

These arguments are the core of the theory of [[set-systems]] and [[hypergraphs]] with restricted intersections. The modular Frankl–Wilson theorem gives explicit graphs for [[ramsey]] theory, where random constructions from the [[probabilistic-method]] are otherwise the main source; it also shows that the chromatic number of $\mathbb R^n$ grows exponentially, and Kahn and Kalai used it in 1993 to disprove Borsuk's conjecture ([[discrete-geometry]]). Eigenvalues of graph matrices ([[eigen]], [[spectral-theorem]]) give further bounds in [[extremal-graphs]]. The polynomial form of the dimension argument reached additive combinatorics in 2016: Croot, Lev and Pach used it for $(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z)^n$, and Ellenberg and Gijswijt then showed that subsets of $\mathbb F_3^n$ without three-term arithmetic progressions have at most $c^n$ elements for some constant $c < 3$ ([[additive-combinatorics]], [[arithmetic-progressions]]).

1. Reverse Oddtown: suppose every $|A_i|$ is even and every $|A_i \cap A_j|$ with $i \ne j$ is odd. Prove that $m \le n + 1$. (Compute $(J - I)^2$ over $\mathbb F_2$.)
2. Let $p$ be a prime. Suppose $p \nmid |A_i|$ for every $i$ and $p \mid |A_i \cap A_j|$ for all $i \ne j$. Prove that $m \le n$.
3. Prove that the multilinear polynomials of degree at most $s$ in $n$ variables form a space of dimension $\sum_{i=0}^s\binom ni$, and that a polynomial and its multilinear reduction agree on $\{0,1\}^n$.
4. Bound the size of a family of subsets of $[n]$ in which every two distinct members share exactly $0$ or $2$ elements, and compare the bound with $n^2$.
